1. Don't Put Your Resume Ahead of the Requirements

作者：Nitin Borwankar

As engineers we sometimes recommend  technologies, methodologies, and approaches for solving problems because deep down we want to have these on our resume, not because they are the best solution for the problem. Such decisions very rarely result in happy outcomes.

作为工程师，我们有时会推荐某些技术、方法论和方案来解决问题，因为内心深处我们想把它们写进简历，而不是因为它们是这个问题的最佳解。这种决策很少有好结果。

The best thing for your career is a long string of happy customers eager to recommend you because you did the right thing by them and for the project. This goodwill will serve you orders of magnitude better than the latest shiny object in the latest shiny language or the latest shiny paradigm. While it is important, even critical, to stay abreast of the latest trends and technologies, this should never happen at the cost of the customer. It’s important to remember that you have a fiduciary duty. As an architect you have been entrusted with the wellbeing of your organization, and it’s expected that you will avoid all conflicts of interest and give the organization your undivided loyalty. If the project isn’t cutting edge or challenging enough for your current career needs, then find one that is.

对你职业生涯最好的投资，是一长串满意的客户——因为你对他们、对项目做了正确的事，他们乐意向别人推荐你。这份善意比最新潮语言、最新潮范式里的最新潮工具好用几个数量级。紧跟最新趋势和技术很重要、甚至关键，但绝不能以牺牲客户为代价。要记住你负有受托责任。作为架构师，组织把福祉托付给你，期望你回避一切利益冲突、对组织倾注全部忠诚。如果这个项目对你当前职业发展不够前沿、不够有挑战，那就去找一个够格的。

If you can’t do that and you are forced to be involved in such a project, then you and everyone else will be happier using the right technology for the customer rather than for your resume. It’s often difficult to resist utilizing a solution that is new and cool, even when it’s inappropriate for the current situation.

如果做不到、你被迫参与这样的项目，那你和所有人都会更快乐——用对客户合适的技术，而不是对简历合适的技术。要克制用一个又新又酷的方案，即使当前场景并不合适，往往并不容易。

With the right solution, the project will have a happier team, a happier customer, and far less stress overall. This will often give you time to go deeper into the existing older technology or to learn the new stuff on your own time. Or to go take that painting class you always wanted to. Your family will love you for it, too—they’ll notice the difference when you get home.

用对方案，项目会有更开心的团队、更开心的客户、整体压力小得多。这往往让你有时间在现有老技术里钻得更深，或者用自己的时间学新东西。或者去上你一直想上的绘画课。你的家人也会因此更爱你——你回家时他们会感觉到不同。

Always put the customer’s long-term needs ahead of your own short-term needs and you won’t go wrong.

永远把客户的长期需求放在自己短期需求之前，你就不会走错。

2. Simplify Essential Complexity; Diminish Accidental Complexity

作者：Neal Ford

Essential complexity represents the difficulty inherent in any problem. For example, coordinating a nation’s air traffic is an inherently complex problem. Every plane’s exact position (including altitude), speed, direction, and destination must be tracked in real time to prevent mid-air and runway collisions. The flight schedules of aircraft must be managed to avoid airport congestion in a continuously changing environment—a severe change in weather throws the entire schedule out of whack.

本质复杂度是问题本身固有的难度。比如协调一个国家的空中交通，本质上就是个复杂问题。每架飞机的精确位置（含高度）、速度、方向、目的地都必须实时跟踪，才能防止空中和跑道相撞。航班时刻必须在持续变化的环境里调度以避免机场拥堵——天气剧变会把整个时刻表打乱。

Conversely, accidental complexity grows from the things we feel we must build to mitigate essential complexity. The antiquated air traffic control system used today is an example of accidental complexity. It was designed to address the essential complexity of controlling the traffic of thousands of airplanes, but the solution itself introduces its own complexity. In fact, the air traffic control system used today is so complex that updating it has proven difficult, if not impossible. In much of the world, air traffic is guided by technology that is more than 30 years old.

反过来，偶然复杂度来自那些我们为了缓解本质复杂度而觉得必须建出来的东西。今天还在用的老旧空管系统就是偶然复杂度的例子：它为了解决「管制几千架飞机」这个本质复杂度而设计，但方案本身又引入了新的复杂度。事实上，今天的空管系统复杂到升级它都困难、甚至不可能。世界上很多地方的空中交通还靠 30 多年前的技术引导。

Many frameworks and vendor “solutions” are the symptoms of the accidental complexity disease. Frameworks that solve specific problems are useful. Overengineered frameworks add more complexity than they relieve.

很多框架和厂商「解决方案」就是偶然复杂度病的症状。解决特定问题的框架是有用的；过度工程的框架带来的复杂度比它缓解的还多。

Developers are drawn to complexity like moths to a flame—frequently with the same result. Puzzle solving is fun, and developers are problem solvers.

开发被复杂度吸引，像飞蛾扑火——结果常常也一样。解谜很有趣，而开发者就是解题的人。

Who doesn’t like the rush of solving some incredibly complex problem? In large-scale software, though, removing accidental complexity while retaining the solution to the essential complexity is challenging.

谁不喜欢解决一个异常复杂问题时的那种快感？但在大规模软件里，去掉偶然复杂度、同时保留对本质复杂度的解，是有挑战的。

How do you do this? Prefer frameworks derived from working code rather than ones cast down from ivory towers. Look at the percentage of code you have in a solution that directly addresses the business problem versus code that merely services the boundary between the application and the users. Cast a wary eye on vendor-driven solutions. They may not be inherently bad, but vendors often push accidental complexity. Make sure that the solution fits the problem.

怎么做？优先选从真实工作代码里长出来的框架，而不是象牙塔里拍下来的。看看你方案里直接解决业务问题的代码占比，对比那些只是在应用和用户边界上打杂的代码。对厂商推动的方案保持警惕。它们未必本质上坏，但厂商常常推销偶然复杂度。确保方案匹配问题。

It’s the duty of the architect to solve the problems inherent in essential complexity without introducing accidental complexity.

架构师的职责是解决本质复杂度固有的问题，同时不引入偶然复杂度。

3. Chances Are, Your Biggest Problem Isn't Technical

作者：Mark Ramm

Right now someone’s running a failing project to build a payroll system. Probably more than one someone.

此刻就有人正在跑一个失败的工资系统项目。很可能不止一个。

Why? Was it because they chose Ruby over Java, or Python over Smalltalk? Or because they decided to use Postgres rather than Oracle? Or did they choose Windows when they should have chosen Linux? We’ve all seen technology take the fall for failed projects. But what are the chances that the problem was really so difficult to solve that Java wasn’t up the the task?

为什么？是因为选了 Ruby 而不是 Java、Python 而不是 Smalltalk？是因为用 Postgres 而不是 Oracle？还是该选 Linux 却选了 Windows？我们都见过技术为失败项目背锅。但问题真的难到 Java 都搞不定的概率有多大？

Most projects are built by people, and those people are the foundation for success and failure. So, it pays to think about what it takes to help make those people successful.

大多数项目是由人建的，人是成败的根基。所以想想怎么帮这些人成功是值得的。

Equally, there’s a good chance that there’s someone who you think is “just not doing it right” and is undermining the project. In these cases, the technology you need to solve your problem is very old and well established indeed; in fact, it’s possibly the most important technical innovation in the history of humanity. What you need is a conversation .

同样，很可能有那么个人，你觉得他「就是没做对」，在拖累项目。这种情况下，你需要的「技术」非常古老而成熟；事实上，它可能是人类历史上最重要的技术创新。你需要的是一场对话。

Mere familiarity with the conversation as a technology isn’t enough. Learning to treat people with respect, and learning give them the benefit of the doubt, is one of the core skills that turn a smart architect into an effective one.

光熟悉「对话」这门技术还不够。学会尊重人、学会先假设对方是善意的，是把聪明架构师变成高效架构师的核心技能之一。

There’s lots more to it than this, but a couple of small tips can significantly increase your conversational effectiveness:

这背后还有很多东西，但几个小技巧能显著提升对话效果：

Approach these events as conversations—not as confrontations. •

把这些场合当对话——而不是对抗。

If you assume the best about people and treat this situation as an opportunity to ask questions, you definitely learn more, and are less likely to put people on the defensive.

如果你对人做最好的假设、把这场景当提问机会，你一定学到更多，也更少把人逼到防御姿态。

Approach these conversations only after you’ve got your attitude right. •

只有在心态摆正后才开始对话。

If you’re angry, frustrated, annoyed, or otherwise flustered, it’s very likely that the other person will interpret your nonverbals as an indication that you’re on the attack.

如果你愤怒、挫败、烦躁、心慌，对方很可能把你的肢体语言解读成你在攻击。

Use these as opportunities to set mutually agreed-upon goals. •

把这些场合当设定共同目标的机会。

Instead of telling a developer that they need to be quiet in meetings because they never let anybody speak, ask if they can help you increase other people’s participation. Explain that some people are more introverted and need longer silences before they enter into a conversation, and ask the developer to help you out by waiting five seconds before jumping in.

不要直接告诉开发「你会上太吵、从不让别人说话」，而是问他能不能帮你提高别人的参与度。解释说有些人更内向、进入对话前需要更长的沉默时间，请他帮个忙——开口前等五秒。

If you start with a shared purpose, treat people “problems” as an opportunity to learn, and manage your own emotions, you’ll not only become more effective, you’ll also discover that you learn something every time.

如果你从共同目的出发、把人的「问题」当学习机会、管理好自己的情绪，你不仅会更高效，还会发现每次都学到东西。

Mark Ramm Mark Ramm is BDFL for TurboGears 2, a python enthusiast, and a generally crazy dude. He’s done nearly every job imaginable from software architect to network administrator to lobster-trap thrower and biker-bar cleaner. He is passionate about making tools that help professional and amateur programmers more productive.

4. Communication Is King; Clarity and Leadership, Its Humble Servants

作者：Mark Richards

All too often, software architects sit in their ivory towers, dictating specifications, technology decisions, and technology direction to the developers below. More often than not, this leads to dissension in the ranks, quickly followed by a revolt by the masses, finally resulting in a software product that doesn’t even come close to resembling the original requirements. Every software architect should know how to communicate the goals and objectives of a software project. The key to effective communication is clarity and leadership.

软件架构师经常坐在象牙塔里，向下属开发口述规格、技术决策和技术方向。这往往导致队伍里出现不满，接着是群众造反，最后交付一个和原始需求八竿子打不着的软件产品。每个软件架构师都该知道怎么传达软件项目的目标和目的。高效沟通的关键是清晰和领导力。

Clarity describes how you communicate. No one on your team is going to read a 100-page architecture decisions document. Being clear and concise in the way you communicate your ideas is vital to the success of any software project. Keep things as simple as possible at the start of a project, and by all means do not start writing lengthy Word documents. Use tools like Visio to create simple diagrams to convey your thoughts. Keep them simple, for they will almost certainly be changing frequently. Another effective means of communication is informal whiteboard meetings. Nothing gets your ideas across better than bringing a group of developers (or other architects) into a room and whiteboarding your ideas. Also, be sure to have a digital camera with you at all times. Nothing is more frustrating than being pushed out of a meeting room with all of your ideas stuck on a whiteboard. Snap a picture, download it, and share it via a wiki with the rest of the team. Throw away the lengthy Word documents and focus more on getting your ideas across, and afterward worry about recording the details of your architectural decisions.

清晰是你怎么沟通。团队里没人会读一份 100 页的架构决策文档。清楚简洁地表达想法，对任何软件项目的成功都至关重要。项目初期把事情尽量简化，千万别一上来就写冗长的 Word 文档。用 Visio 之类的工具画简单的图来传达想法。保持简单，因为它们几乎肯定会频繁变化。另一种高效沟通方式是非正式白板会议。没有什么比把一群开发（或其他架构师）拉进一个房间、在白板上画出你的想法更能传达思路。另外，随身带个数码相机。没有什么比被赶出会议室、想法全留在白板上更令人沮丧。拍下来、下载、通过 wiki 分享给团队。扔掉冗长的 Word 文档，先专注把想法传达出去，之后再记架构决策的细节。

One thing most software architects fail to realize is that a software architect is also a leader. As a leader, you must gain the respect of your co-workers to work in a healthy and effective environment. Keeping developers in the dark about the big picture or why decisions were made is a clear recipe for disaster. Having the developer on your side creates a collaborative environment whereby decisions you make as an architect are validated. In turn, you get buy-in from developers by keeping them involved in the architecture process. Work with developers, not against them. Keep in mind that all team members (e.g., the QA team, business analysts, and project managers, as well as developers) require clear communication and leadership. Employing clarity and demonstrating effective leadership will improve communication and create a strong and healthy work environment.

大多数软件架构师没意识到的一点是：架构师也是领导者。作为领导，你必须赢得同事的尊重，才能在健康高效的环境里工作。让开发对大局和决策原因一无所知，明显是灾难配方。让开发站在你这边，能创造协作环境——你作为架构师做的决策会被验证。反过来，让开发参与架构过程，你能获得他们的认同。和开发一起工作，而不是对着干。记住所有团队成员（QA、业务分析师、项目经理，以及开发）都需要清晰的沟通和领导力。运用清晰、展现高效领导力，会改善沟通、创造强大健康的工作环境。

If “Communication Is King,” then clarity and leadership are its humble ­servants.

如果「沟通为王」，那清晰和领导力就是它谦卑的仆人。

5. Application Architecture Determines Application Performance

作者：Randy Stafford

Application architecture determines application performance. That might seem rather obvious, but real-world experience shows that it’s not. For example, software architects frequently believe that simply switching from one brand of software infrastructure to another will be sufficient to solve an application’s performance challenges. Such beliefs may be based on a vendor’s benchmark trumpeting, say, 25% better performance than the closest competition’s. But if the vendor’s product performs an operation in three milliseconds while the competition’s product takes four milliseconds, the 25% or one-millisecond advantage matters little in the context of a highly inefficient architecture at the root of an application’s performance characteristics.

应用架构决定应用性能。这话听起来很明显，但现实经验表明大家并不真这么认为。比如，软件架构师经常相信只要把软件基础设施从一个品牌换到另一个，就足以解决应用性能问题。这种信念可能基于某厂商的基准测试宣传，说比最接近的竞品好 25%。但如果厂商产品做一个操作要 3 毫秒、竞品要 4 毫秒，那 25% 或 1 毫秒的优势，在一个根上就高度低效的架构面前几乎无足轻重。

In addition to IT managers and vendor benchmarking teams, other groups of people—vendor support departments and authors of application performance management literature—recommend simply “tuning” the software infrastructure, by fiddling with memory allocations, connection pool sizes, thread pool sizes, and the like. But if the deployment of an application is insufficiently architected for the expected load, or if the application’s functional architecture is too inefficient in its utilization of computing resources, then no amount of “tuning” will bring about the desired performance and scalability characteristics. Instead, a re-architecting of internal logic or deployment strategy, or both, will be required.

除了 IT 经理和厂商基准团队，另一群人——厂商支持部门和应用性能管理文献的作者——建议只要「调优」软件基础设施，调调内存分配、连接池大小、线程池大小之类。但如果应用部署没有为预期负载做足够架构设计，或者应用功能架构在利用计算资源上太低效，那多少「调优」都带不来期望的性能和扩展性。反而需要对内部逻辑或部署策略（或两者）重新架构。

In the end, all vendor products and application architectures are constrained by the same fundamental principles of distributed computing and underlying physics: applications, and the products they use, run as processes on computers of limited capacity, communicating with one another via protocol stacks and links of nonzero latency. Therefore people need to appreciate that application architecture is the primary determinant of application performance and scalability. Those quality attributes cannot be miraculously improved with some silver-bullet switch of software brands, or infrastructure “tuning.” Instead, improvements in those areas require the hard work of carefully considered (re-)architecting.

归根结底，所有厂商产品和应用架构都受同样的分布式计算基本原理和底层物理规律约束：应用及其所用产品以进程方式跑在容量有限的计算机上，通过协议栈和非零延迟的链路互相通信。因此大家要认识到：应用架构是应用性能和扩展性的首要决定因素。这些质量属性不可能靠换个软件品牌的银弹开关、或者基础设施「调优」奇迹般改善。相反，这些方面的改进需要艰苦工作——慎重地（重）做架构。

6. Seek the Value in Requested Capabilities

作者：Einar Landre

Often customers and end users state what they think is a viable solution to a problem as a requirement. The classic story on this was told by Harry Hillaker, the lead designer of the F-16 Falcon. His team was asked to design a Mach 2–2.5 aircraft, which was then, and probably still is, a nontrivial task— especially when the objective is to create a “cheap” lightweight aircraft. Consider that the force required to overcome drag quadruples when doubling the speed, and what impact that has on aircraft weight.

客户和最终用户经常把他们认为可行的解决方案当作需求提出来。这方面经典故事来自 F-16 战隼的主设计师 Harry Hillaker。他的团队被要求设计一架马赫 2–2.5 的飞机，这在当时（可能现在仍然）不是个简单任务——尤其目标还是造一架「便宜」的轻型飞机。想想：速度翻倍，克服阻力所需的力变成四倍，对飞机重量又意味着什么。

When the design team asked the Air Force why it needed Mach 2–2.5, the answer was “to be able to escape from combat.” With the real need on the table, the design team was able to address the root problem and provide a working solution: an agile aircraft with a high thrust-to-weight ratio, providing acceleration and maneuverability, not maximum speed.

当设计团队问空军为什么需要马赫 2–2.5，答案是「为了能从战斗中逃脱」。真实需求摆上桌面后，设计团队就能解决根问题、给出可行方案：一架高推重比的敏捷飞机，提供加速度和机动性，而不是最大速度。

This lesson should be brought into software development as well. By asking for the intended value of a requested feature or requirement, architects are able to address the real problem, and hopefully provide a better and cheaper solution than that suggested by the client. The focus on value also simplifies prioritization: the most valuable requirements become the driving requirements.

这个教训也该带进软件开发。通过追问一个被要求的功能或需求的预期价值，架构师能解决真正的问题，并有望提供比客户建议的更好、更便宜的方案。聚焦价值还能简化优先级排序：最有价值的需求成为驱动性需求。

So, how to proceed then? In many ways the required approach is found in the agile manifesto: “Collaboration over contract.” Practically speaking, this implies arranging workshops and meetings where the architects’ focus is on customer needs—helping the customers to answer the “why” question. Be aware that answering the “why” question can be difficult because we very often talk about tacit knowledge. Discussions on how to provide a technical solution should be avoided in these workshops, because they move the focus away from the customer’s domain and into the domain of software development.

那该怎么做？所需方法在很多方面就在敏捷宣言里：「协作高于合同」。实操上，这意味着组织工作坊和会议，让架构师聚焦客户需求——帮客户回答「为什么」。要注意回答「为什么」可能很难，因为我们经常在讨论的是隐性知识。这些工作坊里应避免讨论怎么提供技术方案，因为那会把焦点从客户领域移到软件开发领域。

Einar Landre Einar Landre is a practicing software professional with 25 years’ experience as a developer, architect, manager, consultant, and author/presenter. Currently for StatoilHydro’s Business Application Services, he engages in businesscritical application development, architecture reviews, and software process improvement activities, specializing in SOA, domain-driven design, use of multiagents and design of large-scale, networked, software-intensive systems.

Einar Landre Einar Landre 是有 25 年经验的实践者，做过开发、架构师、经理、顾问和作者/讲者。目前在 StatoilHydro 的业务应用服务部，从事关键业务应用开发、架构评审和软件过程改进，专精 SOA、领域驱动设计、多智能体应用以及大规模网络化软件密集系统的设计。

7. Stand Up!

作者：Udi Dahan

As architects, many of us have grown from highly technical positions where our success was derived mainly from our ability to talk to machines. However, in the role of architect much of our communication is now done with our fellow human beings. Whether it’s talking to developers about the benefits of employing a specific pattern, or explaining to management the cost-benefit tradeoffs of buying middleware, communication is core to our success.

作为架构师，我们很多人是从高度技术的岗位成长起来的，那时成功主要来自和机器对话的能力。但在架构师角色里，大部分沟通是和人。无论是和开发讲用某个模式的好处，还是向管理层解释买中间件的成本收益权衡，沟通都是成功的核心。

Although it’s difficult to measure an architect’s impact on a project, this much is clear: if developers consistently ignore an architect’s guidance and management doesn’t buy in to his recommendations, the “rightness” of his guidance will do little to advance his career. Experienced architects understand that they need to “sell” their ideas and need to communicate effectively in order to do that.

虽然很难衡量架构师对项目的影响，但有一点清楚：如果开发持续无视架构师的指导、管理层不接受他的建议，那他指导的「正确性」对他的职业发展帮助甚微。有经验的架构师明白他们需要「推销」自己的想法，需要高效沟通来做到这一点。

Many books have been written on the topic of interpersonal communication, but I wanted to call out one simple, practical, easy-to-employ tip that will drastically increase the effectiveness of your communication, and, consequently, your success as an architect. If you’re in any situation where you’re talking to more than one person about your guidance, stand up. Whether it’s a formal design review, or an informal discussion over some diagrams, it doesn’t matter. Stand up, especially if everyone else is sitting down.

关于人际沟通的书已经很多，但我想特别提一个简单、实用、容易上手的技巧，它会大幅提升沟通效果，进而提升你作为架构师的成功率：当你在任何场合对多个人讲你的指导时，站起来。不管是正式设计评审还是围着图讨论，无所谓。站起来——尤其当其他人都坐着的时候。

Standing up automatically communicates authority and self-confidence. You command the room. People will interrupt you less. All that is going to make a big difference to whether or not your recommendations will be adopted.

站起来自动传达权威和自信。你掌控整个房间。别人更少打断你。所有这些都会对你的建议是否被采纳产生重大影响。

You’ll also notice that once you stand, you’ll start making more use of your hands and other body language. When speaking to groups of 10 or more people, standing up will also help you make eye contact with everybody. Eye contact, body language, and other visual elements account for a large portion of communication. Standing up also tends to change your tone of voice, volume, pitch, and speed: projecting your voice to larger rooms, slowing down to make more important points. These vocal elements contribute substantially to the effectiveness of communication.

你还会注意到，一旦站起来，你会开始更多用手和其他肢体语言。对 10 人以上讲话时，站起来还能帮你和每个人眼神接触。眼神接触、肢体语言和其他视觉元素在沟通中占很大比例。站起来还会改变你的语调、音量、音高和语速：把声音投射到更大的房间，放慢以强调重点。这些声音要素对沟通效果贡献很大。

The easiest way to more than double your effectiveness when communicating ideas is quite simply to stand up.

把沟通想法的效率提升一倍以上，最简单的办法就是站起来。

Udi Dahan Udi Dahan is The Software Simplist, recognized by Microsoft Corporation with the coveted Most Valuable Professional award for Solutions Architecture now three years running. Udi is a connected technologies advisor working with Microsoft on WCF, WF, and Oslo. He also serves on the Advisory Boards of the Microsoft Software Factories Initiative and the Patterns & Practices’ Prism Project. He provides clients all over the world with training, mentoring, and high-end architecture consulting services, specializing in service-oriented, scalable, and secure .NET architecture design.

Udi Dahan Udi Dahan 是「软件简化者」，连续三年获微软 solutions architecture 方向的 MVP（最有价值专家）奖。他是连接技术顾问，和微软在 WCF、WF、Oslo 上合作。他还任职于微软软件工厂计划顾问委员会和 Patterns & Practices 的 Prism 项目顾问委员会。他为全球客户提供培训、辅导和高端架构咨询，专精面向服务、可扩展、安全的 .NET 架构设计。

8. Everything Will Ultimately Fail

作者：Michael Nygard

Hardware is fallible, so we add redundancy. This allows us to survive individual hardware failures, but increases the likelihood of having at least one failure present at any given time.

硬件会出错，所以我们加冗余。这让我们能扛住单个硬件故障，但也增加了任何时刻都至少有一个故障存在的概率。

Software is fallible. Our applications are made of software, so they’re vulnerable to failures. We add monitoring to tell us when the applications fail, but that monitoring is made of more software, so it too is fallible.

软件会出错。我们的应用由软件构成，所以它们也脆弱。我们加监控来告诉我们应用何时挂了，但监控是更多软件做的，所以也会出错。

Humans make mistakes; we are fallible also. So, we automate actions, diagnostics, and processes. Automation removes the chance for an error of commission, but increases the chance of an error of omission. No automated system can respond to the same range of situations that a human can.

人会犯错；我们也会出错。所以我们把动作、诊断、流程自动化。自动化消除了「做错事」的机会，但增加了「漏做」的机会。没有任何自动化系统能像人一样应对同样范围的情况。

Therefore, we add monitoring to the automation. More software, more opportunities for failures.

于是我们又给自动化加监控。更多软件，更多故障机会。

Networks are built out of hardware, software, and very long wires. Therefore, networks are fallible. Even when they work, they are unpredictable because the state space of a large network is, for all practical purposes, infinite. Individual components may act deterministically, but still produce essentially chaotic behavior.

网络由硬件、软件和很长的线构成。所以网络也会出错。即使网络在工作，它也不可预测，因为大型网络的状态空间在实际意义上是无限的。单个组件可能按确定性方式工作，但合起来本质上是混沌行为。

Every safety mechanism we employ to mitigate one kind of failure adds new failure modes. We add clustering software to move applications from a failed server to a healthy one, but now we risk “split-brain syndrome” if the cluster’s network acts up.

我们为缓解一种故障而加的每个安全机制，都引入新的故障模式。我们加集群软件把应用从故障服务器迁到健康服务器，但现在如果集群网络抽风，我们就冒「脑裂」的风险。

It’s worth remembering that the Three Mile Island accident was largely caused by a pressure relief value—a safety mechanism meant to prevent certain types of overpressure failures.

值得记住：三里岛事故很大程度上是由一个泄压阀引起的——那本来是防止某种超压故障的安全机制。

So, faced with the certainty of failure in our systems, what can we do about it?

所以面对系统必然出故障这个事实，我们能做什么？

Accept that, no matter what, your system will have a variety of failure modes. Deny that inevitability, and you lose your power to control and contain them. Once you accept that failures will happen, you have the ability to design your system’s reaction to specific failures. Just as auto engineers create crumple zones—areas designed to protect passengers by failing first—you can create safe failure modes that contain the damage and protect the rest of the system.

接受这一点：无论如何，你的系统都会有多种故障模式。否认这种必然性，你就失去了控制和遏制它们的能力。一旦接受故障会发生，你就能设计系统对特定故障的反应。就像汽车工程师设计溃缩区——通过先损毁来保护乘客——你可以创造安全故障模式，把损害控制住、保护系统其余部分。

If you do not design your failure modes, then you will get whatever unpredictable—and usually dangerous—ones happen to emerge.

如果你不设计故障模式，那你就会得到任何不可预测、而且通常很危险的、碰巧冒出来的故障模式。

Michael Nygard Michael Nygard wrote Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software (Pragmatic Bookshelf), which won a Jolt Productivity award in 2008. His other writings can be found at http://www.michaelnygard.com/blog.

Michael Nygard Michael Nygard 著有《Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software》（Pragmatic Bookshelf），获 2008 年 Jolt 生产力奖。其他文章见 michaelnygard.com/blog。

9. You're Negotiating More Often Than You Think

作者：Michael Nygard

We’ve all been hit with budgetecture. That’s when sound technology choices go out the window in favor of cost-cutting. The conversation goes something like this.

我们都遭遇过「预算架构」：合理的技术选择被扔出窗外，让位给砍成本。对话大概是这样：

“Do we really need X?” asks the project sponsor.

「我们真的需要 X 吗？」项目资助方问。

For “X”, you can substitute nearly anything that’s vitally necessary to make the system run: software licenses, redundant servers, offsite backups, or power supplies. It’s always asked with a sort of paternalistic tone, as though the grown-up has caught us blowing all our pocket money on comic books and bubble gum, while the serious adults are trying to get on with buying more buckets to carry their profits around in.

「X」可以替换成任何让系统跑起来的关键东西：软件许可、冗余服务器、异地备份、或者电源。问这话总带着一种家长式语气，好像大人撞见我们把零花钱全花在漫画和泡泡糖上，而严肃的大人们正忙着买更多桶来装他们的利润。

The correct way to answer this is “Yes. We do.” That’s almost never the response.

正确回答是「是的，我们需要。」但几乎从来不是这个答案。

After all, we’re trained as engineers, and engineering is all about making tradeoffs. We know good and well that you don’t really need extravagances like power supplies, so long as there’s a sufficient supply of hamster wheels and cheap interns in the data center. So instead of saying, “Yes. We do,” we say something like, “Well, you could do without a second server, provided you’re willing to accept downtime for routine maintenance and whenever a parity bit flips, causing a crash, but if we get error-checking parity memory then we get around that, so we just have to worry about the operating system crashing, which it does about every three-point-nine days, so we’ll have to do nightly restart. The interns can do that whenever they get a break from the powergenerating hamster wheels.”

毕竟我们是工程师训练出来的，工程就是做权衡。我们很清楚你并不真的需要电源这种奢侈品，只要数据中心里有足够多的仓鼠轮和便宜实习生就行。所以我们不说「是的我们需要」，而是说：「嗯，没有第二台服务器也行，只要你愿意接受例行维护停机、以及每次奇偶校验位翻一下导致崩溃；但如果我们买错误校验奇偶内存就能绕过这个，那只需担心操作系统崩溃——大概每 3.9 天崩一次——所以我们每晚重启。实习生从发电仓鼠轮那边歇下来时可以顺便做。」

All of which might be completely true, but is utterly the wrong thing to say. The sponsor stopped listening right after the word “Well.”

这一切可能完全是真的，但完全是错误的回答方式。资助方在「嗯」那个字之后就不听了。

The problem is that you see your part as an engineering role, while your sponsor clearly understands he’s engaged in a negotiation. We’re looking for a collaborative solution-finding exercise; they’re looking for a win-lose tactical maneuver. And in a negotiation, the last thing you want to do is make concessions on the first demand. In fact, the right response to the “do we really need” question is something like this:

问题在于你把自己的角色看作工程，而资助方清楚地知道他在进行一场谈判。我们在找协作式求解；他们在找赢-输战术动作。而在谈判中，你最不该做的就是在第一个要求上让步。事实上，对「我们真的需要吗」这个问题的正确回答大概是：

“Without a second server, the whole system will come crashing down at least three times daily, particularly when it’s under heaviest load or when you are doing a demo for the Board of Directors. In fact, we really need four servers so we can take one HA pair down independently at any time while still maintaining 100% of our capacity, even in case one of the remaining pair crashes unexpectedly.”

「没有第二台服务器，整个系统每天至少崩三次，尤其在负载最重、或者您给董事会做演示的时候。事实上我们需要四台服务器，这样任何时候都能独立取下一个高可用对，同时保持 100% 容量——即使剩下那对里有一台意外崩溃。」

Of course, we both know you don’t really need the third and fourth servers. This is a counter-negotiating gambit to get the sponsor to change the subject to something else. You’re upping the ante and showing that you’re already running at the bare, dangerous, nearly irresponsible minimum tolerable configuration. And besides, if you do actually get the extra servers, you can certainly use one to make your QA environment match production, and the other will make a great build box.

当然我们都知道你并不真的需要第三、第四台服务器。这是一个反谈判策略，让资助方把话题换到别的地方。你在加注，并表明你已经在跑那个光秃秃、危险、几乎不负责任的最低可容忍配置。再说，如果你真多拿到了服务器，一台可以让 QA 环境和生产一致，另一台做构建机正好。

10. Quantify

作者：Keith Braithwaite

“Fast” is not a requirement. Neither is “responsive.” Nor “extensible.” The primary reason why not is that you have no objective way to tell if they’re met. But still users want them. The architect’s role is largely to help the system have these qualities, and to balance the inevitable conflicts and inconsistencies between them. Without objective criteria, architects are at the mercy of capricious users (“no, I won’t accept it, still not fast enough”) and of obsessive programmers (“no, I won’t release it, still not fast enough”).

「快」不是一个需求。「响应灵敏」也不是。「可扩展」也不是。主要原因是你没有客观方法判断它们是否被满足。但用户还是想要这些。架构师的角色很大程度上就是帮系统具备这些品质，并平衡它们之间不可避免的冲突和不一致。没有客观标准，架构师就只能任凭反复无常的用户（「不，我不接受，还是不够快」）和强迫症程序员（「不，我不发布，还是不够快」）摆布。

As with all requirements, we seek to write down these desires. Too often then the vague adjectives come out: “flexible,” “maintainable,” and the rest. It turns out that in every case (yes, even “usable,” with effort), these phenomena can be quantified and thresholds set. If this is not done, then there is no basis for acceptance of the system by its users, valuable guidance is stolen from its builders as they work, and the vision is blurred for those architecting it.

和所有需求一样，我们想把这些愿望写下来。太多时候写出的是模糊形容词：「灵活」「可维护」等等。事实证明，在每一种情况下（是的，连「可用」在内，花点功夫），这些现象都可以量化、设定阈值。不这样做，用户就没有验收系统的依据，建设者在工作时被偷走宝贵指导，做架构的人愿景模糊。

Some simple questions to ask: How many? In what period? How often? How soon? Increasing or decreasing? At what rate? If these questions cannot be answered, then the need is not understood. The answers should be in the business case for the system and if they are not, then some hard thinking needs to be done. If you work as an architect and the business hasn’t (or won’t) tell you these numbers, ask yourself why not. Then go get them. The next time someone tells you that a system needs to be “scalable,” ask that person where new users are going to come from and why. Ask how many and by when? Reject “Lots” and “soon” as answers.

问几个简单问题：多少？在什么周期内？多频繁？多快？在增加还是减少？以什么速率？如果这些问题答不上来，说明需求没被理解。答案应该写在系统的业务论证里；如果没有，就得好好想想。如果你是架构师而业务没告诉（或不肯告诉）你这些数字，问问自己为什么。然后去拿到。下次有人告诉你系统需要「可扩展」，问他新用户从哪来、为什么。问多少、什么时候。拒绝「很多」「很快」这种回答。

Uncertain quantitative criteria must be given as a range: the least, the nominal, and the most. If this range cannot be given, then the required behavior is not understood. As an architecture unfolds, it can be checked against these criteria to see if it is (still) in tolerance. As the performance against some criteria drifts over time, valuable feedback is obtained. Finding these ranges and checking against them is a time-consuming and expensive business. If no one cares enough about the system being “performant” (neither a requirement nor a word) to pay for performance trials, then more than likely performance doesn’t matter. You are then free to focus your architectural efforts on aspects of the system that are worth paying for.

不确定的量化标准必须以区间给出：最小、标称、最大。给不出区间，说明所需行为没被理解。随着架构展开，可以对照这些标准检查它是否（还）在容差内。当某些指标随时间漂移时，你就得到有价值的反馈。找出这些区间并对照检查，是耗时耗钱的事。如果没人在乎系统是否「高性能」（这既不是需求也不是一个词）到愿意为性能试验付钱，那性能大概就不重要。你就可以把架构精力放在值得花钱的方面。

“Must respond to user input in no more than 1,500 milliseconds. Under normal load (defined as…), the average response time must be between 750 and 1,250 milliseconds. Response times less than 500 milliseconds can’t be distinguished by the user, so we won’t pay to go below that.” Now that’s a requirement .

「必须在 1500 毫秒内响应用户输入。正常负载下（定义为……）平均响应时间必须在 750 到 1250 毫秒之间。低于 500 毫秒用户分辨不出来，所以我们不会花钱压到那以下。」这才叫需求。

Keith Braithwaite After many years as an amateur, Keith Braithwaite was first paid to write software in 1996. After that first job, maintaining a compiler built with lex and yacc, he progressed first to modelling microwave propagation for GSM network planning, then seasonal variations in demand for air freight, in C++. A move to consultancy (and Java) introduced him to CORBA and then EJB, and then what was called at the time “e-commerce.” He is currently a principal consultant with Zuhlke and manages its Centre of Agile Practice.

Keith Braithwaite Keith Braithwaite 做了多年业余后，1996 年第一次靠写软件赚钱。第一份工作是维护一个用 lex 和 yacc 构建的编译器。之后他先做 GSM 网络规划中的微波传播建模，再用 C++ 做航空货运需求的季节性变化。转到咨询（和 Java）后接触到 CORBA、EJB，以及当时所谓的「电子商务」。他目前是 Zuhlke 的首席顾问，管理其敏捷实践中心。
